resources.title: SC Secretary of State — Business Filings
resources.description: Official SC portal for business name searches, Articles of Incorporation filing, and charitable solicitation registration.
resources.simpleExplanation: This is the main SC government website where you officially register your nonprofit. You go here to check if your name is available and to file the documents that make your organization a legal entity in South Carolina.

resources.title: IRS EIN Online Application
resources.description: Apply for your Employer Identification Number (EIN) directly through the IRS. The EIN is your organization's federal tax ID — you need it to open a bank account, hire staff, and apply for grants.
resources.simpleExplanation: Think of this as your nonprofit's Social Security Number. It's free, takes about 10 minutes online, and you get it instantly. You cannot do almost anything official — bank accounts, grants, taxes — without it.

resources.title: IRS Form 1023-EZ — Streamlined 501(c)(3) Application
resources.description: The streamlined application for federal tax-exempt status under section 501(c)(3). Available for organizations with projected annual gross receipts under $50,000. Filed through pay.gov with a $275 fee.
resources.simpleExplanation: This is the filing that makes donations to your nonprofit tax-deductible and unlocks most foundation and government grants. The EZ version is a shorter form for smaller organizations — about 3 pages instead of 30. Once the IRS approves it (usually 2-4 weeks), your nonprofit is officially tax-exempt.

resources.title: SC Department of Revenue — Nonprofit Exemptions
resources.description: Information on South Carolina state tax exemptions for nonprofits, including sales tax exemptions. After receiving your federal 501(c)(3) determination, you can apply for SC state tax exemption here.
resources.simpleExplanation: After you get your federal 501(c)(3) status, you also need to register with the state of South Carolina. This can make your organization exempt from SC state sales tax — meaningful savings when you're buying supplies and equipment for programs.

resources.title: SC Charitable Solicitation Registration
resources.description: South Carolina requires charities that solicit donations in the state to register with the Secretary of State's office. Required before you begin fundraising.
resources.simpleExplanation: Before you ask anyone in South Carolina for a donation — on your website, at an event, or in an email — you legally need to register as a charity in SC. It's a simple registration through the Secretary of State and costs about $50.

resources.title: aiEDU — AI Education Project
resources.description: A nonprofit dedicated to expanding access to AI education, particularly for underserved communities. Offers free curriculum resources, educator training, and partnership programs for organizations running AI literacy programming.
resources.simpleExplanation: aiEDU builds the curriculum so you don't have to start from scratch. They have free, classroom-tested materials for teaching AI to people with no technical background. A partnership here gives you instant curriculum credibility and their network.

resources.title: Center on Innovation (CORI)
resources.description: A nonprofit focused on building tech ecosystems and digital opportunity in underserved communities across America. Runs the Innovation Initiative, produces research on tech access gaps, and connects entrepreneurs with resources.
resources.simpleExplanation: CORI is doing nationally what you want to do in South Carolina. They focus specifically on areas being left behind in the tech economy. They have data, relationships, and a playbook that's directly relevant — and they're always looking for strong regional partners.

resources.title: Google AI Education Resources
resources.description: Free AI learning resources from Google, including the Machine Learning Crash Course, Teachable Machine, and educator resources for bringing AI concepts to classrooms and community programs.
resources.simpleExplanation: Google has invested heavily in free AI education materials. These are polished, beginner-friendly, and you can use them in your workshops without building everything yourself. The Teachable Machine tool is especially good for hands-on, no-code AI demos.

resources.title: Microsoft AI Skills Initiative
resources.description: Microsoft's global initiative to train 25 million people in AI skills. Includes free learning paths on LinkedIn Learning, Azure AI Fundamentals certification resources, and a nonprofit partnership program.
resources.simpleExplanation: Microsoft has committed serious resources to AI education and actively looks for nonprofit partners to extend their reach into underserved communities. Their free learning paths are well-structured for beginners, and they have a formal program for partnering with organizations like yours.

resources.title: OpenAI Foundation — People-First AI Fund
resources.description: OpenAI's philanthropic arm focused on ensuring AI benefits humanity broadly. The People-First AI Fund specifically supports organizations helping communities navigate AI's impact on work, society, and equity. Watch for application windows.
resources.simpleExplanation: This is your most important grant target. OpenAI is putting money directly into organizations doing exactly what you're building — helping communities that might be left behind by AI. The grants are significant and the alignment is perfect. Monitor this page constantly.

resources.title: Google.org — Nonprofits and Social Impact
resources.description: Google's philanthropic arm funds nonprofits using technology and innovation to address society's biggest challenges. Also administers the Google for Nonprofits program with free Google Workspace and $10K/month in Google Ads.
resources.simpleExplanation: Google.org funds a lot of work at the intersection of technology and equity. Beyond direct grants, the Google for Nonprofits program (free Workspace + $10K/month in ads) is something you should apply for the day you have your 501(c)(3) letter.

resources.title: USDA Rural Business Development Grant (RBDG)
resources.description: USDA grant program funding technical assistance and training for small businesses and communities. Grants range from $10,000 to $500,000. Targeted at projects that strengthen economies and business capacity.
resources.simpleExplanation: AI literacy training for entrepreneurs and workers fits this grant perfectly. The USDA has money specifically for teaching communities skills that help their businesses and economy. The range is wide — even a small $25K grant from here funds a solid pilot program.

resources.title: NSF — Advancing Informal STEM Learning (AISL)
resources.description: National Science Foundation program funding projects that advance public understanding of STEM, including AI. Supports community-based learning, exhibits, media, and workforce development for underserved populations.
resources.simpleExplanation: The NSF funds organizations that teach science and technology to the public outside of formal schools. Your workshops and community programs fit this category. NSF grants are larger and more competitive, but they carry enormous credibility that opens other doors.

resources.title: EDA — Economic Development Administration Grants
resources.description: Federal grants through the Department of Commerce's Economic Development Administration. Funds workforce development, innovation ecosystems, and technology adoption in economically distressed communities.
resources.simpleExplanation: EDA funds projects that create jobs and build economic capacity in communities that need it most. Your AI incubator (Phase 2) is a natural fit for EDA funding — you're building the economic infrastructure for SC to compete in the AI economy.

resources.title: Nonprofit Bylaws Template — IRS-Compliant
resources.description: The National Council of Nonprofits provides guidance on creating bylaws that comply with IRS requirements and state law. Bylaws govern how your organization is structured, how decisions are made, and how the board operates.
resources.simpleExplanation: Your bylaws are the rulebook for how your nonprofit operates. You need them before your first board meeting and before filing for 501(c)(3) status. Don't write them from scratch — use an existing template and customize it. This link explains what you need and why.

resources.title: IRS Conflict of Interest Policy Template
resources.description: The IRS provides a sample Conflict of Interest Policy in the appendix of Publication 4221. Having a COI policy is strongly recommended (and basically expected) for 501(c)(3) organizations to maintain their tax-exempt status.
resources.simpleExplanation: A Conflict of Interest policy protects your organization by setting rules for what board members and staff have to disclose when they have a personal financial interest in a decision. The IRS literally gives you a template to use — this is one document you don't have to think hard about.

resources.title: Board Meeting Minutes Template
resources.description: Template and guidance for recording nonprofit board meeting minutes. Minutes are the official legal record of your board's decisions and are required for nonprofit governance compliance.
resources.simpleExplanation: Every board meeting needs documented minutes — they're the legal record that your organization is being governed properly. If you ever get audited or need to prove you ran things by the book, minutes are the evidence. Use a template so you don't miss anything required.

resources.title: Nonprofit Mission Statement Examples and Framework
resources.description: Guidance and examples for crafting an effective nonprofit mission statement. A strong mission statement is the foundation of your 501(c)(3) application, all grant writing, and your public communications.
resources.simpleExplanation: Your mission statement is the one or two sentences that explain why your nonprofit exists. It needs to be specific enough to be meaningful and broad enough to cover everything you want to do. This resource walks you through how to write a good one with real examples.

resources.title: SC Innovation Network (SCRIN)
resources.description: SCRIN (through the SC Office of Health) works to improve economic and health outcomes in South Carolina. Has deep community trust, established relationships with organizations across the state, and experience running programs in underserved areas.
resources.simpleExplanation: SCRIN is your most important early partner in SC. They already have the trust of South Carolina communities you want to reach — trust that takes years to build. A relationship here means you can run your first workshops in communities that already know and trust your partner, rather than showing up cold.

resources.title: Benedict College — BCSIA
resources.description: Benedict College's Center for Science Innovation and Athletics (BCSIA) and broader STEM programs in Columbia, SC. Historically Black College and University (HBCU) with strong community ties in underserved SC communities.
resources.simpleExplanation: Benedict is an HBCU in Columbia with deep ties to Black communities across SC. A partnership here creates a natural pathway to communities that have historically been excluded from tech and innovation. Being associated with an HBCU also strengthens your equity story for grant applications.

resources.title: SC Research Authority / SC Launch
resources.description: The South Carolina Research Authority (SCRA) and its SC Launch program support technology-based companies and entrepreneurs in South Carolina. Provides funding, mentorship, and connections to the state's tech and research ecosystem.
resources.simpleExplanation: SCRA is one of the main engines of the SC tech economy. SC Launch specifically funds early-stage tech ventures. While they primarily back for-profit companies, they're a central node in the SC innovation network and worth knowing — especially for Phase 2 of your plan.

resources.title: VentureSouth
resources.description: Angel investor network across the Southeast with strong SC presence. Invests in early-stage technology companies and has chapters in Columbia, Greenville, and other SC cities.
resources.simpleExplanation: VentureSouth is the main angel investor network in SC. They're relevant to Phase 3 of your plan (the community investment fund) — understanding how they work and building relationships with their members will help you design your own angel fund program and possibly find investors for companies in your incubator.

resources.title: USC/Columbia Technology Incubator
resources.description: University of South Carolina's technology incubator and innovation programs in Columbia. Provides space, mentorship, and university resources to early-stage companies and social enterprises. Alumni of USC have a natural advantage in accessing these programs.
resources.simpleExplanation: As a USC alum, you have an in here that most people don't. The incubator is physical space where early-stage ventures work, meet each other, and get connected to university resources, faculty, and the Columbia business community. Walk in and introduce yourself.

resources.title: Beaufort Digital Corridor
resources.description: Economic development initiative in the Beaufort, SC area focused on growing the tech and digital economy in the Lowcountry. Connects tech companies, entrepreneurs, and talent in the Beaufort-Hilton Head region.
resources.simpleExplanation: If your work in the Lowcountry is going to be connected to any local tech infrastructure, the Beaufort Digital Corridor is the main node. They work to bring tech economic development to a region that's often overshadowed by Charleston and Columbia.

resources.title: ADAPT SC / SC EPSCoR
resources.description: SC EPSCoR (Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research) and the ADAPT program support research and innovation in South Carolina, particularly in underserved areas. Funded by NSF to build SC's research capacity.
resources.simpleExplanation: SC EPSCoR exists specifically because SC has historically been underrepresented in federal research funding. They have NSF dollars to help build SC's capacity in science and technology — which aligns with building AI literacy in communities. They can also be a bridge to larger NSF grants down the road.
